newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia may import Western grain -trade.
newsitem.headline: Russia may import Western grain -trade.

text.p: Russia may import European and U.S. grain due to its own poor harvest and low output in neighbouring countries, grain sources said on Thursday.
A source at a Western commodities house said he thought Russia's Far East could buy up to 500,000 tonnes of U.S. hard red winter wheat for delivery in November or December.

"No deals have been struck, but they will probably go through Roskhleboprodukt (the semi-state buying agency)," the source said. "The Far East's got the money, and don't ask me from where because I don't know."
He said Roskhleboprodukt, which declined to discuss imports, was also "actively interested" in maize (corn).
Analysts said relatively high domestic prices could also encourage imports.
A tonne of Russian third-class soft milling wheat costs about 900,000 roubles ($166) ex-farm gate, and $240 once it is shipped to Moscow and value-added tax is figured in.

"We're seeing a point where domestic Russian wheat prices may be higher than world prices, which means Russia won't be inclined to export and may be inclined to buy," said independent agriculture specialist Andrei Sizov of SovEcon Ltd.

Trade sources said other possible imports by Russia would probably not happen until 1997, well after Moscow officials have digested the results of harvests in Siberia and the former Soviet republics of Kazakhstan and Ukraine.
"There's a lot of talk about imports now," Sizov said. "I think we'll see some changes in import patterns, with Russia buying a greater share of grain from Western countries than in previous years."
The former breadbaskets of Ukraine and Kazakhstan are forecasting bad harvests that could leave them with some grain to sell to Russia, but less than in previous years.

Sizov said almost half of Russia's wheat flour imports came from Ukraine and 12 percent from Kazakhstan over the past 12 months. Sixty percent of Russia's wheat imports came from Kazakhstan over the same period.
Deliveries from Kazakhstan, Ukraine and Eastern Europe helped Russia offset its 1995 net harvest of 63.4 million tonnes, the worst in three decades.

"The situation in Kazakhstan and Ukraine is not very good for Russia this year, although Russia will try to import from there," Sizov said. "But Europe is looking more attractive, especially with those (European Union) export subsidies."
Agriculture Minister Viktor Khlystun has said Russia may import 4.0-4.5 million tonnes of feedgrains, mostly maize and soymeal, and 500,000 tonnes of food wheat, from North America or Australia.
Russia's grains harvest so far is 63.5 million tonnes gross. Crops from eight million ha have yet to be brought in, mostly from Siberia where rain may have lowered yields.
Kazakhstan has harvested a net nine million tonnes of grain so far, with about 75 percent of the total grain crop in.

Officials forecast the net Kazakh harvest at 16.5 million tonnes, far above last year's official 10 million. But trade sources say the higher level may be unrealistic, unless farmers have greatly under-reported results.
Kazakhstan will export grain in excess of the six million tonnes it needs to meet annual domestic demand -- but it may not be enough for Russia.

Ukraine's grain harvest, excluding maize, is nearly over, and stands at nearly 21.3 million tonnes gross, with maize output to reach up to two million tonnes and private farmers producing an additional 1-2 million tonnes of grain.
Kiev said earlier on Thursday Ukraine's total harvest would be 27 million tonnes, far below last year's official 36.5 million tonnes.
Trade sources say the result is likely to be closer to 26 million tonnes, and Kiev has quietly banned exports until its reserves are filled.
